title: Materials science
note: Engineering materials fall into four families: metals (strong, ductile, conductive), ceramics (hard, brittle, heat resistant), polymers (light, flexible, easy to shape), and composites, which combine materials to get properties neither has alone. Atomic bonding and crystal structure explain much of this behavior.

read.title: Why materials behave as they do
text: A material's behavior begins with its atoms. In a metal, outer electrons are shared across the whole crystal, which is why metals conduct heat and electricity. The bonds are not tied to particular neighbors, so planes of atoms can slip past one another along line defects called dislocations. That slip is plastic deformation, and it makes metals ductile.

Metal atoms pack into regular crystals. Iron at room temperature is body-centered cubic, with each atom touching eight neighbors. Aluminum and copper are face-centered cubic, with twelve neighbors and about 74% of space filled, the densest possible packing of equal spheres.

Ceramics hold their atoms with strong ionic and covalent bonds that resist slip. They are hard and survive high temperatures, but a small crack can run through them, so they are brittle. Polymers are long chain molecules; they are light and easy to mold but much less stiff than metals.

Composites combine these strengths. In carbon-fiber reinforced polymer, stiff fibers carry the load while an epoxy matrix holds them in place. In reinforced concrete, steel bars carry the tension that concrete cannot.
